title: The Executive Document must describe every action in future-conditional language
content:
A.1.10.2.4.8.3.7 requires that each item "uses future-conditional language and clearly outlines the actions that will take place if the Executive Proposal passes. For example, phrasing such as 'If this Executive Proposal passes, then this action will take place' ensures clarity and avoids ambiguity."

Prescribing grammar looks fussy until you consider the alternative. "The Stability Fee is increased to 6%" reads as a decision already taken and is a natural way to write from an Executive Sheet full of imperative instructions. A voter skimming such a document sees a changelog, not a ballot — and the framing quietly implies that voting is a formality rather than the operative act.

The conditional form encodes the actual state of the world at publication: nothing has happened, and whether it happens depends on the reader. Every sentence restates that the vote is causal.

It also guards against a subtler leak. The Executive Document is written *after* the GovOps meeting has reached consensus, the Content Liaisons have confirmed, and the Spell has been crafted. Everyone in the process treats the content as settled, and that certainty naturally bleeds into the prose. A mandated conditional is a mechanical defence against process momentum being communicated to voters as a fait accompli.
description: A.1.10.2.4.8.3.7 prescribes the grammar — 'If this Executive Proposal passes, then this action will take place' — so the document can never be misread as reporting a settled fact.
